analysis.one_liner: Expands tribal borrowing, pension, and leasing powers and cuts taxes to spur economic development in Indian country.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to five House committees and never received a hearing or a vote before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would give tribal governments tools other governments already have: the ability to issue tax-exempt bonds for community projects, treatment of tribal employee pension plans as governmental plans, and freedom from some federal loan taxes. It would offer tech companies located on tribal lands a tax credit of $3,000 per full-time employee for supplying domestically made technology to the federal government, let tribes lease their restricted lands without Interior Department sign-off, and let tribes combine funding from several federal programs into one development project. One provision cuts the other way: it would remove businesses owned by tribes on tribal lands from the National Labor Relations Act, meaning employees at those businesses would lose federal rights to organize unions and bargain collectively. The bill died without any action after being sent to five committees.
analysis.who_benefits: Tribal governments and the roughly one million people living in Indian country, one of the poorest regions in the United States. Tribes would gain cheaper borrowing for schools, housing, and infrastructure through tax-exempt bonds, more control over leasing their own land, and the ability to pool fragmented federal program money into single development projects. Tribal employees would keep more of their pay, since student loan repayments for Indian Health Service and Bureau of Indian Education workers would no longer be taxed as income. Tech companies that open on tribal lands and supply American-made technology to the federal government would get a $3,000 per-employee tax credit [S2][S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Tribal governments and residents of Indian country

how_it_helps.text: Tribal governments could issue tax-exempt bonds when most proceeds fund an essential government function or facilities on the reservation, with an explicit ban on using them to finance Class II or III gaming buildings, lowering borrowing costs for community infrastructure [S3].

Tribal government pension plans would be treated the same as state and local government plans under the tax code and ERISA, which they currently are not when employees perform commercial activities [S2][S3].

Student loan repayments for Indian Health Service workers and Bureau of Indian Education employees who work with students would be excluded from taxable income, letting tribal schools and health programs attract staff [S2][S3].

Any tribe — not just the Navajo Nation — could lease restricted Indian lands in specified circumstances without approval from the Secretary of the Interior, and tribes could ask federal agencies to consolidate assistance from multiple programs into a single development project, with the affected agency required to consult and decide within 90 days [S2][S3].

Tech companies located in Indian country that supply the federal government with domestically sole-sourced technology would get a $3,000 tax credit per covered full-time employee, an incentive to locate jobs on tribal lands [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The federal treasury would forgo tax revenue from the bond interest exclusion, the tech company credit, and the loan repayment exclusions. Workers at tribally owned businesses on tribal lands would bear a real cost: they would lose federal collective bargaining and union organizing rights under the National Labor Relations Act. Federal agencies would also have to waive some of their own statutes and rules at tribal request for consolidated projects [S2][S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal treasury; workers at tribally owned businesses

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts enterprises owned and operated by a tribe on its lands from the National Labor Relations Act, so roughly all workers at tribally owned casinos, hotels, and other commercial businesses on tribal lands would lose federal rights to form unions and bargain collectively [S2][S3].

Title IX directs the head of any federal agency to waive statutory provisions, regulations, and procedures identified in a tribal application, unless the waiver conflicts with the program's purposes or a provision specifically governing Indian programs — a broad waiver authority that could sweep aside rules that protect project beneficiaries [S3].

Extending the Navajo Nation's existing leasing authority to all tribes would remove Interior Department approval as a checkpoint on transactions involving restricted Indian lands, which supporters frame as tribal self-determination and skeptics could frame as reduced federal oversight of trust lands [S2][S3].

The tech tax credit is a targeted corporate tax expenditure that only helps companies tied to federal sole-source defense-related contracts, narrowing its benefit to a small set of firms rather than tribal economies generally [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For tribal residents the bill's core provisions — cheaper bonds, pension parity, untaxed loan repayments, and consolidated federal funding — address real barriers to development in one of the country's poorest regions. The serious trade-off is the labor law carve-out: it removes federal union rights from employees of tribally owned businesses, and a worker who loses bargaining rights cannot easily be made whole by growth elsewhere. A fair reading is that the bill trades worker protections for tribal sovereignty and development incentives, which tribes themselves have often sought; the waiver authority is broad but subject to stated limits. On balance it is designed to help a disadvantaged population, but it is not costless for workers in tribally owned commercial enterprises.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and immediately referred to five different House committees, then to four subcommittees, and none of them ever held a hearing, marked it up, or voted on it before the 112th Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Representative Tom Cole, a Republican from Oklahoma, introduced the bill on April 15, 2011 [S1][S5].

The Speaker referred it not to one committee but to five — Ways and Means, Education and the Workforce, Natural Resources, Financial Services, and Judiciary — with each to consider only the provisions in its jurisdiction [S5].
Between April and August 2011 it was further referred to four subcommittees, including Indian and Alaska Native Affairs, and no further action was ever recorded [S5].
No other House member cosponsored the bill [S4], and it never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The bill's death left the status quo intact: tribally owned businesses remain exempt from federal labor law disputes in practice because of litigation over the National Labor Relations Act's application to tribal enterprises, tribal pension and bond rules remain narrower, and the federal treasury keeps the forgone revenue. No committee had to cast a recorded vote on a package mixing tribal development incentives with a labor law exemption.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tribal business status quo and the federal treasury

for.name: Rep. Tom Cole
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Indian Country Economic Development Act on April 15, 2011

against.name: Speaker of the House
against.role: Presiding officer who assigns bills to committees
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to five committees at once, each with jurisdiction over only part of it, a routing that made comprehensive action unlikely

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and zero cosponsors from either party, and it never advanced far enough for a vote that would show a partisan split [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Tribal government enterprises and tribal economies
industries.note: The bill would expand tribal bonding authority, put tribal pensions on equal footing with other government plans, speed land leasing, and let tribes pool federal program funds, all aimed at development in one of the country's poorest regions. The gains flow to tribal governments and their members rather than to a private industry.

industries.industry: Tech companies supplying federal contracts from Indian country
industries.note: A new $3,000-per-employee tax credit would reward companies that locate on tribal lands and supply domestically made, sole-sourced technology to the federal government. It creates jobs where the credit is used but is also a targeted federal tax expenditure.

industries.industry: Organized labor and workers at tribally owned businesses
industries.note: By removing tribally owned enterprises on tribal lands from the National Labor Relations Act, the bill would end federal union organizing and collective bargaining rights for their employees. Labor's interest here runs alongside the workers it represents.

Tribal governments' expanded access to tax-exempt bonds would open a new borrowing market that underwriters service. Cheaper tribal borrowing also funds schools, housing, and infrastructure for residents.

industries.industry: Federal land management (Bureau of Indian Affairs)
industries.note: The bill would let tribes lease restricted lands without Interior Department approval in specified circumstances and require a report on tribes taking over land title records functions. That shifts functions from federal hands to tribal control.
